note: Categorises 283 benchmarks into general, domain specific and target specific, a map for choosing evidence.
title: A Survey on Large Language Model Benchmarks
explain_beginner: With hundreds of different tests now used to grade AI language models, the question is how anyone is supposed to know which test actually measures what they care about. The paper reviews 283 separate AI benchmarks and sorts them into a clear map, tests of general skill like reasoning and knowledge, tests built for specific fields like law, medicine or writing code, and tests aimed at narrower concerns like safety or an AI agent's ability to complete multi-step tasks. Rather than inventing a new test, the authors organize the existing landscape so people can find the right kind of evidence for a given question. They also point out serious problems across the field, some AI models may have already seen benchmark questions during training, which inflates their apparent scores, and many tests are unfairly harder for languages other than English. The paper argues current tests are also weak at capturing dynamic, real-world situations rather than fixed multiple-choice questions.
explain_business: For anyone buying or evaluating AI models based on benchmark scores, this survey is a useful checklist for treating those scores with some skepticism. It confirms a concern practitioners already suspect, that impressive numbers on well-known benchmarks can be inflated because test questions leaked into a model's training data, and that stated performance may not transfer well outside English or outside a benchmark's narrow question format. Buyers evaluating vendor claims should ask which specific benchmark was used, whether it is domain-specific to their actual use case such as legal work or coding, and whether it tests dynamic or multi-step agent behavior rather than static multiple-choice questions, since a static score may say little about real-world reliability. The paper does not change what any model can actually do. Its value is as a reference for building a more rigorous internal evaluation checklist before trusting a single headline benchmark number from a vendor pitch.
explain_practitioner: The method is a systematic literature survey covering 283 large language model evaluation benchmarks, organized into a three-tier taxonomy of general capability, domain-specific, and target-specific benchmarks rather than any new empirical evaluation of models. The general category spans core linguistics, knowledge and reasoning tests, the domain-specific category covers natural sciences, humanities and social sciences, and engineering, and the target-specific category covers risk and reliability testing plus agent evaluation. The result that matters is less a single number than a diagnosis of the benchmark ecosystem, the authors highlight training-test data contamination that inflates reported scores, cultural and linguistic bias that disadvantages non-English and morphologically complex languages, over-reliance on outcome-only scoring that penalizes correct reasoning with small errors, and a shortage of benchmarks capturing dynamic, evolving tasks rather than static questions. A limitation the authors effectively acknowledge is that the paper does not fully spell out its own selection criteria for which 283 benchmarks were included, and a landscape review like this risks aging quickly as new benchmarks appear constantly.
